article_title: Situational judgement testing at different stages of undergraduate medical training and the risk of professionalism lapses: A cohort study.
citation: Sahota G, Tiffin PA, Smith D, Tyrrell E, Hampshire M, Taggar J. (2026). Situational judgement testing at different stages of undergraduate medical training and the risk of professionalism lapses: A cohort study. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.70020
title: Administer professionalism SJTs during training rather than before admission, with professionalism-specific content and low cognitive load
description: The article's policy implication is that traditionally designed SJT-format assessments work better as developmental and selection tools during, not before, medical training. It states that "SJTs designed with professionalism‐specific content and a low cognitive load are those most likely to demonstrate incremental predictive validity over existing academic metrics", and that care should be taken to reduce cognitive load so scores add value above academic ability.
requirements: SJT content mapped to the professionalism curriculum or standards being assessed
cognitive load low enough that scores are not redundant with academic and cognitive metrics
constraints: Findings come from a single institution, so the authors advise caution in generalising to other settings
the evidence for construct-driven pre-admission SJTs as alternatives is not yet established
examples: The Nottingham Medical School administered a mandatory summative professionalism SJT at the end of second year, which independently predicted lapse odds in this cohort
